entries.title: Blake Plateau: the largest known deep-sea coral reef
paragraphs: In January 2024, NOAA Ocean Exploration and a coalition of partners (Ocean Exploration Trust, the University of New Hampshire, the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, Temple University and the U.S. Geological Survey) announced the results of a multi-year mapping campaign: a nearly continuous province of cold-water coral mounds on the Blake Plateau, off the south-eastern United States, that is the largest known deep-sea coral reef habitat on Earth.

Published as Sowers et al. 2024 in the journal Geomatics, the study synthesised 31 multibeam sonar surveys and 23 submersible dives gathered over more than a decade. The full coral province stretches up to about 500 km long and 110 km wide, with an especially dense core area -- nicknamed 'Million Mounds' -- some 254 km long and 42 km wide. Across the full study region, automated mapping classified 83,908 mound-like peaks. The nearly continuous coral province covers roughly 6.4 million acres, an area larger than Vermont.

The province lies beneath the Gulf Stream at depths commonly described as roughly 500–1,000 m. Currents carry food to cold-water corals that live below the sunlit zone and feed on drifting organisms and organic particles.

What you see here: the seabed is real bathymetry from the GMRT Synthesis, showing genuine relief consistent with the mapped mound field, though at this tile's resolution (roughly 53 x 61 m per cell) individual coral colonies and the smallest mounds are not resolved.

entries.title: A dense coral mound cluster
paragraphs: This stretch of seabed shows real, mapped terrain relief consistent with the dense mound clusters described across the wider Blake Plateau province -- roughly 72 m of local relief around this point, with depths in the low 700s to high 700s of metres nearby.

Coral skeletons and rubble accumulate into mounds with relief commonly measured in tens of metres. The regional mapping study combined sonar classification with submersible observations to identify this habitat.
The scan records local terrain relief within the coral province; individual mounds require finer mapping to identify.

entries.title: Desmophyllum pertusum, reef-builder of the deep
paragraphs: Desmophyllum pertusum, formerly known as Lophelia pertusa, is the main reef-building coral described in NOAA's Blake Plateau mapping announcement. Its polyps capture drifting food without symbiotic algae. Healthy Desmophyllum pertusum is naturally white; that colour is not a sign of bleaching. The OBIS export for this tile contains records reported at 585–866 m.

Over thousands of years, generation after generation of coral skeleton accumulates into the mounds you see across this province -- among the slowest-built, longest-lived structures in the ocean, and correspondingly fragile: a single mound can represent millennia of growth that a moment's careless contact could damage.

entries.title: One mound among thousands
paragraphs: This scan samples terrain roughly 294 m southwest of the main cluster marker. The shipped grid reads about 776 m here.
Across the wider study region, Sowers and colleagues classified 83,908 mound-like peaks. A depth reading at this scan point alone does not identify an individual coral mound.

entries.title: The Gulf Stream overhead
paragraphs: The western Blake Plateau is influenced by the Gulf Stream. Water moving across coral habitat carries the organisms and organic particles that cold-water coral polyps capture as food.
The mapping study describes a province extending hundreds of kilometres, with varied mound shapes and distributions rather than uniform coral cover.

facts.label: Role here
facts.value: currents carry suspended food to coral habitat

entries.title: Between the mounds
paragraphs: The grid reads about 780 m at this scan point, lower than the main cluster marker at about 744 m. The regional coral province includes both raised coral habitat and areas of open sediment.
This scan compares nearby terrain depths. Identifying a particular channel between coral mounds requires finer mapping and observations.
